decks.domain: Remaining required equipment and the start of safe driving practices

cards.front: Which children riding in Arizona must be in a child passenger restraint system?
cards.back: Any child younger than eight riding in a vehicle in Arizona has to be properly secured in a child passenger restraint system.

cards.front: What are head restraints on seat backs for?
cards.back: Head restraints on seat backs exist to lower the risk of a whiplash injury when you are hit from behind.

cards.front: Where should an adjustable head restraint sit?
cards.back: An adjustable head restraint should sit against the back of your head, level with the middle of your ear.

cards.front: Where exactly does a head restraint line up?
cards.back: A head restraint lines up with the middle of the ear and touches the back of the head; it is not set to the top of the head or left low at the neck.

cards.front: What must every motor vehicle's muffler do?
cards.back: Every motor vehicle needs a muffler that works well and runs at all times, so it does not cause excessive pollution or unusual noise.

cards.front: Is fitting a muffler cut-out or bypass allowed?
cards.back: Fitting a muffler cut-out, a bypass or any similar device is illegal.

cards.front: Which vehicles must have an exhaust emissions system?
cards.back: Motor vehicles of the nineteen sixty-seven model year or newer must have an exhaust emissions system to help cut air pollution.

cards.front: What must a vehicle's engine be equipped to prevent?
cards.back: The engine of every motor vehicle must be equipped so that excessive fumes and smoke cannot escape.

cards.front: How does the muffler rule differ from the emissions rule?
cards.back: The muffler rule targets noise and pollution and bans bypass devices, while the emissions rule requires an exhaust emissions system on nineteen sixty-seven and newer models.

decks.domain: Remaining required equipment and the start of safe driving practices

cards.front: What must be true of a vehicle's windshield and wipers?
cards.back: A vehicle must have a windshield with no cracks, and its windshield wipers must work properly.

cards.front: What does the manual say about window tint film?
cards.back: Tint film on windows and windshields is legal only within certain limits, so owners should confirm the maker or installer follows Arizona law.

cards.front: Does the manual give exact window tint limits?
cards.back: The manual gives no tint numbers; it says only that tint is lawful within limits and puts the burden on the owner to check that the installer complied.

cards.front: When does a vehicle need a driver-side outside mirror, and what must it show?
cards.back: If a vehicle's build or load blocks the driver's rear view, it needs at least one outside mirror on the driver side showing at least two hundred feet of highway behind.

cards.front: From how far away must your horn be heard?
cards.back: Your vehicle must have a working horn that can be heard from two hundred feet away.

cards.front: What one distance covers both the outside mirror rule and the horn rule?
cards.back: The required outside mirror must show two hundred feet of road behind, and the required horn must be audible at two hundred feet, so one distance covers both rules.

cards.front: Which vehicles may carry a siren, whistle or bell?
cards.back: Emergency vehicles are the ones that may carry a siren, whistle or bell.

cards.front: Which vehicles may show flashing red lights on the front?
cards.back: Flashing red lights on the front of a vehicle are banned, even on a disabled vehicle, except on authorized emergency vehicles, school buses and snow removal equipment.

cards.front: When should you turn on your hazard warning lights?
cards.back: Turn on your hazard warning lights whenever your vehicle is stopped on the roadway or on the shoulder.

cards.front: How do hazard flashers differ from forward flashing red lights?
cards.back: Hazard flashers are switched on when you are stopped on the roadway or shoulder, while flashing red lights facing forward are off-limits to ordinary vehicles even when they break down.

decks.domain: Remaining required equipment and the start of safe driving practices

cards.front: What does defensive driving protect, and where does it start?
cards.back: Driving defensively protects both your life and your driving record, and it starts with constant awareness of conditions and planning ahead.

cards.front: What else does defensive driving mean besides awareness?
cards.back: Defensive driving also means anticipating dangers and acting in time so that you never strike an obstacle or another vehicle.

cards.front: What can follow even a crash with no injuries?
cards.back: Even a crash with no injuries brings inconvenience and repair bills, and it can lead to a court appearance, fines and higher insurance rates.

cards.front: Which driving attitudes does the manual call the most important?
cards.back: The manual names courtesy and consideration for others as the most important driving attitudes and the key to safe driving.

cards.front: What other mental habits matter for safe driving?
cards.back: Concentration and alertness also matter, so make keeping your mind on the road a habit.

cards.front: How does the manual rank courtesy against concentration?
cards.back: Courtesy and consideration are ranked as the most important attitudes, while concentration and alertness are described as other important elements.

cards.front: How dangerous is driving while drowsy or emotionally upset?
cards.back: Driving while drowsy or emotionally upset can be as dangerous as driving impaired.

cards.front: What is foresight in driving?
cards.back: Foresight is the ability to size up a traffic situation quickly and be ready to take corrective action.

cards.front: How does foresight differ from defensive driving as a whole?
cards.back: Foresight is about sizing up a situation fast and being ready to correct, while defensive driving is the wider practice of awareness, planning, anticipation and right action.

cards.front: What will every driver eventually meet, and what prepares you?
cards.back: However many years you have driven, you will eventually meet equipment failures, bad weather, unskilled drivers and drivers who ignore the rules, and defensive driving is the best preparation.

decks.domain: Remaining required equipment and the start of safe driving practices

cards.front: Which defensive habits does the manual list?
cards.back: The defensive habits the manual lists are keeping good vision ahead and around you, staying alert, obeying speed limits and knowing when to slow or stop, and always wearing your safety belt.

cards.front: Where does a defensive driver keep looking?
cards.back: A defensive driver keeps looking ahead and around, checks the mirrors constantly, and watches for hazards in front, at the sides and behind.

cards.front: How does a beginner learn to drive, and who can help outside a program?
cards.back: A beginner learns by instruction, observation and practice, and someone not in a driver training program should ask an experienced, skilled, licensed driver to help.

cards.front: Where should you practice basic control once you hold a permit?
cards.back: Once you hold an instruction permit, practice starting, pulling out of a parking space, stopping and controlling the vehicle in a parking lot or other open area with little traffic.

cards.front: When does beginner practice in an open lot begin?
cards.back: Beginner practice in an open lot comes after the instruction permit is issued, not before it.

cards.front: What problems do experienced drivers often struggle with?
cards.back: Experienced drivers often struggle with carelessness, overconfidence and bad habits that build up over time.

cards.front: What risk does the manual name for experienced drivers?
cards.back: The risk the manual names for experienced drivers is carelessness, overconfidence and old bad habits, not a lack of basic skill.

cards.front: What decides how safe a driver you really are as rules and traffic change?
cards.back: Driving rules and techniques have changed and traffic keeps growing, so how well you adapt decides how safe a driver you really are.

cards.front: How does the manual define a driving skill?
cards.back: The manual defines a driving skill as a rehearsed strategy of anticipating, reacting and constantly adjusting the space between you and other vehicles.

cards.front: How does progress as a driver show?
cards.back: Progress as a driver shows in dropping risk-taking, keeping to speed limits and being able to take corrective action when needed.

decks.domain: Remaining required equipment and the start of safe driving practices

cards.front: Which distractions does the manual tell you to avoid at the wheel?
cards.back: Distractions to avoid at the wheel include reading a GPS or map, using a phone or texting, hunting for a dropped item, tending to children and buckling a safety belt.

cards.front: When should your safety belt be fastened?
cards.back: Fastening a safety belt is on the distraction list only when it is done while driving, so the belt goes on before the vehicle moves.

cards.front: What should you do before using a cell phone or texting?
cards.back: If you need to use a cell phone or send or read a text, first pull safely off the road and stop.

cards.front: Where should your hands be while you drive?
cards.back: While you drive, both hands should be on the steering wheel so you keep full control.

cards.front: What does Arizona law forbid doing with a wireless device while driving?
cards.back: Arizona law forbids holding or supporting a wireless device while driving.

cards.front: Which text and video uses are banned while driving?
cards.back: While driving you may not write or read any text-based message, and you may not watch, record or broadcast video.

cards.front: When may a driver use a wireless device while driving?
cards.back: While driving, a driver may use a wireless device only to report an emergency or for hands-free or voice-to-text operation.

cards.front: Which ways of using a wireless device are permitted while driving?
cards.back: Hands-free and voice-to-text use of a wireless device is permitted.

cards.front: What does the wireless law ban, and what does it still allow?
cards.back: Holding or supporting a device is what the law bans, while hands-free and voice-to-text operation stays allowed.

cards.front: When may you use a wireless device while driving versus pulling off to stop?
cards.back: While driving, wireless device use is limited to reporting an emergency or hands-free or voice-to-text operation; otherwise you must pull safely off the road and stop before using a cell phone or texting.

decks.domain: Remaining required equipment and the start of safe driving practices

cards.front: How do you stay in your lane?
cards.back: To stay in your lane, look well down the road and make only small steering corrections when needed.

cards.front: Where should you look in a curve or turn, and why?
cards.back: Drivers tend to steer toward where they look, so in a curve or turn, looking toward the outside of your lane helps you stay in it.

cards.front: Where do you look on a straight road versus in a curve?
cards.back: On a straight road you look well ahead and make slight corrections, while in a curve you look toward the outside of your lane.

cards.front: What should you scan for, and where especially?
cards.back: Scan for cars, motorcycles, bicyclists, people and animals that may cross your path, especially at intersections, crosswalks, shopping centers, construction areas and playgrounds.

recap_hooks.text: Head restraints sit level with the middle of the ear, mufflers work at all times with no bypass, and newer models carry an emissions system.
The blocked-view mirror and the horn share a two-hundred-foot distance, and hazard lights go on when you stop on the road.
Courtesy and consideration rank first, and foresight helps you size up trouble and act in time.
Beginners practice in an open area after the permit, and experienced drivers guard against carelessness and old habits.
Never hold a phone while driving; use it hands-free, or pull off and stop, except to report an emergency.
Look well ahead on a straight road and toward the outside of your lane in a curve.
